name: Bedroom Coders: Games and Programs Made at Home
description: Elite, Tetris, Elk Cloner, Linux and Minecraft: the games and programs that students and teenagers wrote on their own, and the cheap home computers that let them.

checkpoints.name: Students and hackers
checkpoints.note: MIT students wrote Spacewar in their spare time, student teachers made The Oregon Trail, and a caver wrote Colossal Cave Adventure for his daughters, which inspired Zork. One programmer wrote CP/M largely on his own, and two friends coded VisiCalc, the first spreadsheet for a personal computer.

checkpoints.name: The home computer boom
checkpoints.note: The VIC-20, ZX81, BBC Micro, Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum put a computer in many bedrooms, with Sinclair Research and Acorn Computers leading in Britain, and magazines printed programs to type in. A 15-year-old wrote Elk Cloner, one of the first viruses to spread in the wild, as a prank.

checkpoints.name: Many machines
checkpoints.note: The Amstrad CPC, MSX, Amiga 1000 and Atari ST competed for the bedroom. Two Cambridge students wrote Elite, a whole galaxy on a BBC Micro, Tetris spread from a Moscow computing centre, and in 1986 two brothers in Lahore wrote the Brain virus.

checkpoints.name: From hobby to industry
checkpoints.note: As the PC and its clones won the market the 8-bit machines faded, though the Amiga and Atari ST lasted into the 1990s. In 1991 a Finnish student, Linus Torvalds, began Linux at home as a hobby, and in 2009 a Swedish programmer working alone began Minecraft, which became the best-selling game of all.

checkpoints.name: The heirs
checkpoints.note: The Raspberry Pi, a small, cheap board from a British charity, is often seen as the heir to the BBC Micro, and again invites young people to learn by tinkering. Flappy Bird, made by one developer in Vietnam, topped the app charts in 2014.
